14240.arabic_source:
١٤٢٤٠ — عن أبي جري جابر بن سليم قال: رأيت رجلًا يصدر الناس عن رأيه، لا يقول شيئًا إلا صدروا عنه، قلت: من هذا؟ قالوا: هذا رسول اللّٰه ﷺ. قلت: عليك السلام يا رسول اللّٰه، مرتين. قال:
((لا تقل: عليك السلام، فإن عليك السلام تحية الميت، قل: السلام عليك)).
قال: قلت: أنت رسول اللّٰه؟ قال:
((أنا رسول اللّٰه الذي إذا أصابك ضر فدعوته كشفه عنك، وإن أصابك عام سنة فدعوته أنبتها لك، وإذا كنت بأرض قفراء - أو فلاة - فضلت راحلتك فدعوته ردها عليك)).
قال: قلت: اعهد إلي. قال:
((لا تسبن أحدًا)).
قال: فما سببت بعده حرًّا، ولا عبدًا، ولا بعيرًا، ولا شاة.
قال:
((ولا تحقرن شيئًا من المعروف، وأن تكلم أخاك وأنت منبسط إليه وجهك، إن ذلك من المعروف، وارفع إزارك إلى نصف الساق، فإن أبيت فإلى الكعبين، وإياك وإسبال الإزار، فإنها من المخيلة، وإن اللّٰه لا يحب المخيلة، وإن امرؤ شتمك وعيرك بما يعلم فيك، فلا تعيره بما تعلم فيه، فإنما وبال ذلك عليه)).
صحيح: رواه أبو داود (٤٠٨٤) - واللفظ له -، والترمذي (٢٧٢٢)، والبيهقي في الشعب (٥٧٣٠).
قوله: “عليك السلام تحية الميت” قال الخطابي: “يوهم أن السنة في تحية الميت أن يقال له: عليك السلام كما يفعله كثير من العامة”. وقد ثبت عن النبي ﷺ أنه دخل المقبرة فقال: ((السلام عليكم أهل دار قوم مؤمنين)) فقدم الدعاء على اسم المدعو له كما هو في تحية الأحياء، وإنما قال ذلك القول منه إشارة إلى ما جرت به العادة منهم في تحية الأموات، إذ كانوا يقدمون اسم الميت على الدعاء… فالسنة لا تختلف في تحية الأحياء والأموات”. اهـ.

14240.english_source:
14240 — Abū Jurayy Jābir ibn Sulaym narrated:
I saw a man whose judgment the people followed. He would not say anything except that they acted upon it.
I asked:
“Who is this?”
They replied:
“This is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.”
I said twice:
“Upon you be peace, O Messenger of Allah.”
He said:
“Do not say, ‘Upon you be peace,’ for ‘upon you be peace’ is the greeting of the dead. Rather say: ‘Peace be upon you.’”
I asked:
“Are you the Messenger of Allah?”
He replied:
“I am the Messenger of Allah. He (Allah) is the One whom, if harm afflicts you and you call upon Him, He removes it from you; and if a year of drought afflicts you and you call upon Him, He causes the earth to grow for you; and if you are in a barren land—or wilderness—and your riding animal becomes lost, then you call upon Him and He returns it to you.”
I said:
“Give me some instruction.”
He said:
“Never insult anyone.”
Jābir said:
“After that I never insulted a free person, a slave, a camel, or a sheep.”
Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“Do not belittle any good deed, even speaking to your brother while your face is cheerful toward him, for that is part of goodness. Raise your lower garment to the middle of your shin; if you refuse, then at least to the ankles. Beware of letting the lower garment trail beneath the ankles, for that is from arrogance, and Allah does not love arrogance. If a man insults you and shames you for something he knows about you, do not shame him for something you know about him, for the burden of that will fall upon him.”
Authentic: Narrated by Abū Dāwūd (4084), and this is his wording, al-Tirmidhī (2722), and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān (5730).
Regarding the words, “ʿAlayka al-salām is the greeting of the dead,” al-Khaṭṭābī said:
“This might give the impression that the Sunnah when greeting the dead is to say, ‘ʿAlayka al-salām,’ as many common people do. However, it is authentically established that the Prophet ﷺ entered the graveyard and said: ‘Peace be upon you, inhabitants of the abode of believing people.’ Thus, he placed the supplication before the person being addressed, just as is done when greeting the living. His statement merely referred to the customary manner in which the Arabs used to address the dead, whereby they placed the name of the deceased before the supplication… Therefore, the Sunnah does not differ between greeting the living and greeting the dead.”

14297.arabic_source:
١٤٢٩٧ — عن ابن عمر قال: رأيت رسول اللّٰه ﷺ بفناء الكعبة، محتبيا بيده، هكذا.
صحيح: رواه البخاري (٦٢٧٢).

14297.english_source:
14297 — Ibn ʿUmar narrated:
“I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the courtyard of the Kaʿbah, sitting in the iḥtibāʾ posture (sitting with his knees drawn up toward his body and holding his legs together with his hands), like this.”
Authentic: Narrated by al-Bukhārī (6272).

14482.arabic_source:
١٤٤٨٢ — عن جابر قال: قال رسول اللّٰه ﷺ - أو قال: سمعت رسول اللّٰه ﷺ يقول -:
((إذا انقطع شسع أحدكم - أو من انقطع شسع نعله - فلا يمش في نعل واحدة حتى يصلح شسعه، ولا يمش في خف واحد، ولا يأكل بشماله، ولا يحتبي بالثوب الواحد، ولا يلتحف الصماء)).
صحيح: رواه مسلم (٢٠٩٩: ٧١).
قوله: “شسع” هو سيور النعل، وهو الذي يدخل بين الإصبعين، ويدخل في الثقب الذي في صدر النعل المشدود في الزمام، وجمعه شسوع.

14482.english_source:
14482 — Jābir narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said—or he said, “I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say”:
“If the strap of one of your sandals breaks, do not walk in only one sandal until you repair its strap. Do not walk in only one leather sock, do not eat with your left hand, do not sit in the iḥtibāʾ posture (sitting with the knees drawn up toward the body and held together) while wrapped in a single garment, and do not wrap yourself in the ṣammāʾ manner (wrapping the body tightly in a single garment so that the arms cannot easily emerge; scholars also explained the prohibited form as a one-garment wrap that may expose the ʿawrah).”
Authentic: Narrated by Muslim (2099:71).
The word “shisʿ” refers to the sandal strap that passes between the toes and through the hole at the front of the sandal where it is secured to the upper strap.
Its plural is shusūʿ.

١٤٧٠٠ — عن أبي سعيد الخدري يقول: سمعت رسول اللّٰه ﷺ يقول:
((إن اللّٰه ليسأل العبد يوم القيامة حتى يقول: ما منعك إذ رأيت المنكر أن تنكره؟ فإذا لقن اللّٰه عبدًا حجته قال: يا رب، رجوتك وفرقت من الناس)).
حسن: رواه ابن ماجه (٤٠١٧)، وأحمد (١١٧٣٥)، وصححه ابن حبان (٧٣٦٨). وإسناده حسن من أجل نهار العبدي، فإنه حسن الحديث.
فائدة مهمة: الضوابط في الإنكار على المنكر
قال العلامة ابن القيم في كتابه إعلام الموقعين (٤/٣):
“أن النبي ﷺ شرع لأمته إيجاب إنكار المنكر، ليحصل بإنكاره من المعروف ما يحبه اللّٰه ورسوله، فإذا كان إنكار المنكر يستلزم ما هو أنكر منه وأبغض إلى اللّٰه ورسوله فإنه لا يسوغ إنكاره، وإن كان اللّٰه يبغضه ويمقت أهله، وهذا كالإنكار على الملوك والولاة بالخروج عليهم؛ فإنه أساس كل شر وفتنة إلى آخر الدهر.
فإنكار المنكر أربع درجات: الأولى: أن يزول ويخلفه ضده، الثانية: أن يقل وإن لم يزل بجملته، الثالثة: أن يخلفه ما هو مثله، الرابعة: أن يخلفه ما هو شر منه؛ فالدرجتان الأوليان مشروعتان، والثالثة موضع اجتهاد، والرابعة محرمة.”
(تنبيه في أقوال أهل العلم بشأن الإنكار على الحكام والخروج عليهم:
كلام ابن القيم المتقدم في ذم الخروج المسلح على الحكام وبيان ما قد يترتب عليه من المفاسد يوافق القول الذي صار غالبًا عند أهل السنة، ولا يُفهم منه أن جميع علماء السلف كانوا متفقين على هذا الحكم منذ البداية، أو أن ظلم الحكام لا يجوز إنكاره.

فقد نقل القاضي عياض، كما أورده النووي في شرح صحيح مسلم (١٢/٢٢٩، طبعة دار الكتاب العربي)، وقوع الخلاف في هذه المسألة، وذكر احتجاج بعض أهل العلم بخروج الحسين بن علي، وعبد الله بن الزبير، وأهل المدينة، وجماعة من التابعين مع ابن الأشعث. ونقل كذلك قول جماهير أهل السنة بمنع الخروج على الحكام لمجرد الفسق والظلم، لما يترتب عليه من الفتن وإراقة الدماء. وذكر أن من أهل العلم من حكى أن هذا الخلاف كان أولًا، ثم حصل الإجماع على المنع.

وقال ابن حجر العسقلاني في ترجمة الحسن بن صالح بن حي عند بيان معنى قولهم «كان يرى السيف»: «وهذا مذهب للسلف قديم»، ثم بيّن أن الأمر استقر على ترك الخروج المسلح لما ظهر من عواقبه الأشد، وأن هذا الرأي لا يقدح وحده في عدالة من ثبتت عدالته. انظر: ابن حجر، تهذيب التهذيب (٢/٢٥٠، طبعة دار الفكر).

وعليه، فلا يصح إنكار وقوع الخلاف التاريخي بين أهل العلم، كما لا يصح إغفال ما غلب على قول جمهور المتأخرين من منع قتال الحكام لمجرد ظلمهم وفسقهم، مع بقاء الأحكام الخاصة بالكفر البواح وشروط القدرة والمآلات.

ولا يجوز الخلط بين إنكار ظلم الحاكم باللسان، وترك طاعته في المعصية، وبين الخروج المسلح عليه؛ فهذه مسائل متمايزة. وقد ثبت عن النبي ﷺ قوله: «إِنَّمَا الطَّاعَةُ فِي الْمَعْرُوفِ» رواه البخاري (٧٢٥٧) ومسلم (١٨٤٠). وثبت عنه قوله: «إِلَّا أَنْ تَرَوْا كُفْرًا بَوَاحًا عِنْدَكُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ فِيهِ بُرْهَانٌ» رواه البخاري (٧٠٥٦) ومسلم (١٧٠٩).

فالواجب إنكار الظلم بحسب العلم والاستطاعة، وبالوسائل المشروعة، مع مراعاة المصالح والمفاسد، وعدم تعريض الناس لشر أعظم. ولا تقتضي مراعاة المفاسد تبرير الظلم أو إسقاط حق المظلوم، كما أن وجوب إنكار الظلم لا يجعل كل وسيلة لإزالته جائزة. والله أعلم.)
ثم إن الأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر فرض كفاية، إذا قام به البعض سقط عن الباقي، وإذا تركه الجميع أثم كل من تمكن منه بلا عذر. ثم إنه يتعين على من يتمكن من إزالته، كمن يرى زوجته أو أولاده أو غلامه على منكر.
ويجب الإنكار على المنكر ما أجمع عليه العلماء، وأما المختلف فيه فلا إنكار فيه، لأن على أحد المذهبين إن كل مجتهد مصيب، وهو المختار عند كثير من المحققين، وعلى المذهب الآخر أن المصيب واحد، والمخطئ غير متعين لنا، والإثم موضوع عنه.
والعلماء وعامة المسلمين يشاركون في الأمور الظاهرة، مثل الأمر بالصلاة والصوم، والنهي عن الزنا، وشرب الخمر، والضرب والشتم، ونحو ذلك، وإن كان الأمر يتعلق بدقائق الأفعال والأقوال، وما يتعلق بالاجتهاد، فلا يكون للعوام فيه مدخل، وإنما يكون ذلك للعلماء فقط.
وليس للآمر بالمعروف والناهي عن المنكر البحث والتفتيش والتجسس واقتحام الدور بالظنون، إلا أن يخبره من يثق بقوله: “إن رجلًا خلا برجل ليقتله، أو خلا بامرأة ليزني بها، ويبيع الخمور والحشيش”، فيجوز لهم أن يتجسسوا ويقتحموا حذرًا من فوات ما لا يستدرك.
وقوله: ((فإن لم يستطع فبقلبه)) أي ينكر ذلك بقلبه، ولا يرضى به. وليس فيه إزالة للمنكر وتغييره، ولكن هذا الذي في وسعه، وفي هذا الحديث دليل على أن من خاف على نفسه القتل والضرب والتشريد سقط عنه تغيير المنكر على أصح أقوال أهل العلم.
ويجب أن يكون الإنكار على المنكر سرًّا، قال سليمان الخواص: من وعظ أخاه فيما بينه وبينه فهي نصيحة، ومن وعظ على رؤوس الناس فإنما فضحه. رواه ابن أبي الدنيا في الأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر (رقم ٥٨).
14700.english_display:
14700 — Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī narrated:
I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:
“Allah will question a servant on the Day of Resurrection until He says, ‘What prevented you, when you saw wrongdoing, from condemning it?’ Then, if Allah grants a servant his excuse, he will say, ‘My Lord, I hoped in You, but I feared the people.’”
Good: Narrated by Ibn Mājah (4017), Aḥmad (11735), and authenticated by Ibn Ḥibbān (7368). Its chain is good because Nahār al-ʿAbdī is a transmitter whose hadith is graded good.
Important Benefit: Guidelines for Condemning Wrongdoing
The scholar Ibn al-Qayyim said in Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn (4/3):
The Prophet ﷺ prescribed for his Ummah the obligation of condemning wrongdoing so that, through its condemnation, the good that Allah and His Messenger love may result.
If condemning an evil necessarily leads to something even more evil and more hateful to Allah and His Messenger, then it is not permissible to condemn it in that manner, even though Allah hates the original evil and detests those who commit it. An example of this is condemning the wrongdoing of kings and rulers by rebelling against them, for that is the foundation of every evil and tribulation until the end of time.
Condemning wrongdoing has four levels:
The evil disappears and is replaced by its opposite.
The evil is reduced, even if it does not disappear completely.
It is replaced by another evil equal to it.
It is replaced by something worse than it.
The first two levels are prescribed. The third is a matter of juristic judgment. The fourth is prohibited.
(Scholarly clarification concerning condemning rulers and armed rebellion:
Ibn al-Qayyim's preceding statement concerning the dangers of armed rebellion against rulers represents the position that later became predominant among the scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah. It does not mean that every scholar among the early generations agreed upon this ruling from the beginning, or that rulers' injustice must remain unchallenged.

Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, as quoted by al-Nawawī in Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (vol. 12, p. 229, Dār al-Kitāb al-ʿArabī edition), records the historical disagreement. He mentions that some scholars invoked the actions of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr, the people of Madinah, and groups of the Tābiʿīn who rose alongside Ibn al-Ashʿath. He also records the majority Sunni position prohibiting armed rebellion against rulers merely because of their injustice or sinful conduct, particularly due to bloodshed and disorder. He further reports the view that this earlier disagreement was subsequently followed by consensus against rebellion.

Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, while discussing al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Ḥayy, explicitly acknowledges that permitting armed opposition to unjust rulers was an old position among the Salaf. He then explains that the later position settled against such rebellion because its consequences proved more destructive. He also states that adherence to the earlier opinion does not, by itself, invalidate the established integrity of a scholar. See: Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb (vol. 2, p. 250, Dār al-Fikr edition).

Therefore, the historical disagreement must neither be denied nor confused with the later predominant position. The majority of later Sunni scholars prohibited fighting rulers merely for injustice or sinful conduct, while treating cases of unmistakable disbelief under distinct legal conditions, including ability and consequences.

Furthermore, condemning a ruler's injustice verbally, refusing to obey sinful commands, and attempting armed rebellion are distinct matters. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Obedience is only in what is right.” Narrated by al-Bukhārī (7257) and Muslim (1840). He also established an exception concerning “clear disbelief for which you have proof from Allah.” Narrated by al-Bukhārī (7056) and Muslim (1709).

Thus, injustice must be opposed according to knowledge, ability, and lawful means, while considering likely benefits and harms and avoiding greater evil. Preventing greater harm does not justify oppression or extinguish the rights of those wronged. Equally, the duty to oppose injustice does not make every proposed means of removing it permissible. And Allah knows best.)
Enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is a communal obligation. If some people fulfill it, the obligation falls from the rest. If everyone abandons it, then everyone capable of carrying it out without a valid excuse bears sin.
It becomes an individual obligation upon the one who is able to remove the wrongdoing, such as someone who sees his wife, children, or servant committing a wrong.
Wrongdoing should be condemned in matters upon which the scholars have reached consensus.
As for matters genuinely disputed among the scholars, they are not condemned in the same manner, because according to one position every qualified mujtahid is correct, and this is the view preferred by many verifying scholars. According to the other position, only one view is correct, but the mistaken party is not necessarily identifiable to us, and he is not sinful for his qualified error.
Scholars and ordinary Muslims alike may participate in matters whose rulings are clear and apparent, such as commanding prayer and fasting and forbidding fornication, drinking alcohol, assault, insults, and similar matters.
If, however, the matter concerns subtle details of actions and speech or issues requiring juristic interpretation, ordinary people have no role in that; rather, it belongs to the scholars alone.
The one who enjoins right and forbids wrong has no right to investigate, search, spy, or enter people’s homes merely on the basis of suspicion.
An exception is when a trustworthy person informs him of an imminent grave wrong, such as a man isolating another person in order to kill him, being alone with a woman in order to commit fornication with her, or selling intoxicants and hashish. In such a case, investigation and intervention may be permitted in order to prevent an irreversible harm.
The Prophet’s ﷺ words:
“If he cannot, then with his heart”
mean that he should reject the wrongdoing inwardly and not approve of it.
This does not physically remove or change the wrongdoing, but it is what lies within his ability.
This hadith also indicates, according to the strongest view among the scholars, that if a person fears for himself being killed, beaten, or driven away, the obligation of physically changing the wrongdoing falls from him.
The author states that correction of wrongdoing should be carried out privately.
Sulaymān al-Khawwāṣ said:
“Whoever admonishes his brother privately, between himself and him, has sincerely advised him. Whoever admonishes him publicly before the people has only exposed and disgraced him.”
Narrated by Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Amr bi-al-Maʿrūf wa-al-Nahy ʿan al-Munkar (58).

وقال ابن حجر العسقلاني في ترجمة الحسن بن صالح بن حي عند بيان معنى قولهم «كان يرى السيف»: «وهذا مذهب للسلف قديم»، ثم بيّن أن الأمر استقر على ترك الخروج المسلح لما ظهر من عواقبه الأشد، وأن هذا الرأي لا يقدح وحده في عدالة من ثبتت عدالته. انظر: ابن حجر، تهذيب التهذيب (٢/٢٥٠، طبعة دار الفكر).

وعليه، فلا يصح إنكار وقوع الخلاف التاريخي بين أهل العلم، كما لا يصح إغفال ما غلب على قول جمهور المتأخرين من منع قتال الحكام لمجرد ظلمهم وفسقهم، مع بقاء الأحكام الخاصة بالكفر البواح وشروط القدرة والمآلات.

ولا يجوز الخلط بين إنكار ظلم الحاكم باللسان، وترك طاعته في المعصية، وبين الخروج المسلح عليه؛ فهذه مسائل متمايزة. وقد ثبت عن النبي ﷺ قوله: «إِنَّمَا الطَّاعَةُ فِي الْمَعْرُوفِ» رواه البخاري (٧٢٥٧) ومسلم (١٨٤٠). وثبت عنه قوله: «إِلَّا أَنْ تَرَوْا كُفْرًا بَوَاحًا عِنْدَكُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ فِيهِ بُرْهَانٌ» رواه البخاري (٧٠٥٦) ومسلم (١٧٠٩).

فالواجب إنكار الظلم بحسب العلم والاستطاعة، وبالوسائل المشروعة، مع مراعاة المصالح والمفاسد، وعدم تعريض الناس لشر أعظم. ولا تقتضي مراعاة المفاسد تبرير الظلم أو إسقاط حق المظلوم، كما أن وجوب إنكار الظلم لا يجعل كل وسيلة لإزالته جائزة. والله أعلم.)
ثم إن الأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر فرض كفاية، إذا قام به البعض سقط عن الباقي، وإذا تركه الجميع أثم كل من تمكن منه بلا عذر. ثم إنه يتعين على من يتمكن من إزالته، كمن يرى زوجته أو أولاده أو غلامه على منكر.
ويجب الإنكار على المنكر ما أجمع عليه العلماء، وأما المختلف فيه فلا إنكار فيه، لأن على أحد المذهبين إن كل مجتهد مصيب، وهو المختار عند كثير من المحققين، وعلى المذهب الآخر أن المصيب واحد، والمخطئ غير متعين لنا، والإثم موضوع عنه.
والعلماء وعامة المسلمين يشاركون في الأمور الظاهرة، مثل الأمر بالصلاة والصوم، والنهي عن الزنا، وشرب الخمر، والضرب والشتم، ونحو ذلك، وإن كان الأمر يتعلق بدقائق الأفعال والأقوال، وما يتعلق بالاجتهاد، فلا يكون للعوام فيه مدخل، وإنما يكون ذلك للعلماء فقط.
وليس للآمر بالمعروف والناهي عن المنكر البحث والتفتيش والتجسس واقتحام الدور بالظنون، إلا أن يخبره من يثق بقوله: “إن رجلًا خلا برجل ليقتله، أو خلا بامرأة ليزني بها، ويبيع الخمور والحشيش”، فيجوز لهم أن يتجسسوا ويقتحموا حذرًا من فوات ما لا يستدرك.
وقوله: ((فإن لم يستطع فبقلبه)) أي ينكر ذلك بقلبه، ولا يرضى به. وليس فيه إزالة للمنكر وتغييره، ولكن هذا الذي في وسعه، وفي هذا الحديث دليل على أن من خاف على نفسه القتل والضرب والتشريد سقط عنه تغيير المنكر على أصح أقوال أهل العلم.
ويجب أن يكون الإنكار على المنكر سرًّا، قال سليمان الخواص: من وعظ أخاه فيما بينه وبينه فهي نصيحة، ومن وعظ على رؤوس الناس فإنما فضحه. رواه ابن أبي الدنيا في الأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر (رقم ٥٨).
14700 — Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī narrated:
I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:
“Allah will question a servant on the Day of Resurrection until He says, ‘What prevented you, when you saw wrongdoing, from condemning it?’ Then, if Allah grants a servant his excuse, he will say, ‘My Lord, I hoped in You, but I feared the people.’”
Good: Narrated by Ibn Mājah (4017), Aḥmad (11735), and authenticated by Ibn Ḥibbān (7368). Its chain is good because Nahār al-ʿAbdī is a transmitter whose hadith is graded good.
Important Benefit: Guidelines for Condemning Wrongdoing
The scholar Ibn al-Qayyim said in Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn (4/3):
The Prophet ﷺ prescribed for his Ummah the obligation of condemning wrongdoing so that, through its condemnation, the good that Allah and His Messenger love may result.
If condemning an evil necessarily leads to something even more evil and more hateful to Allah and His Messenger, then it is not permissible to condemn it in that manner, even though Allah hates the original evil and detests those who commit it. An example of this is condemning the wrongdoing of kings and rulers by rebelling against them, for that is the foundation of every evil and tribulation until the end of time.
Condemning wrongdoing has four levels:
The evil disappears and is replaced by its opposite.
The evil is reduced, even if it does not disappear completely.
It is replaced by another evil equal to it.
It is replaced by something worse than it.
The first two levels are prescribed. The third is a matter of juristic judgment. The fourth is prohibited.
(Scholarly clarification concerning condemning rulers and armed rebellion:
Ibn al-Qayyim's preceding statement concerning the dangers of armed rebellion against rulers represents the position that later became predominant among the scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah. It does not mean that every scholar among the early generations agreed upon this ruling from the beginning, or that rulers' injustice must remain unchallenged.

Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, as quoted by al-Nawawī in Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (vol. 12, p. 229, Dār al-Kitāb al-ʿArabī edition), records the historical disagreement. He mentions that some scholars invoked the actions of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr, the people of Madinah, and groups of the Tābiʿīn who rose alongside Ibn al-Ashʿath. He also records the majority Sunni position prohibiting armed rebellion against rulers merely because of their injustice or sinful conduct, particularly due to bloodshed and disorder. He further reports the view that this earlier disagreement was subsequently followed by consensus against rebellion.

Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, while discussing al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Ḥayy, explicitly acknowledges that permitting armed opposition to unjust rulers was an old position among the Salaf. He then explains that the later position settled against such rebellion because its consequences proved more destructive. He also states that adherence to the earlier opinion does not, by itself, invalidate the established integrity of a scholar. See: Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb (vol. 2, p. 250, Dār al-Fikr edition).

Therefore, the historical disagreement must neither be denied nor confused with the later predominant position. The majority of later Sunni scholars prohibited fighting rulers merely for injustice or sinful conduct, while treating cases of unmistakable disbelief under distinct legal conditions, including ability and consequences.

Furthermore, condemning a ruler's injustice verbally, refusing to obey sinful commands, and attempting armed rebellion are distinct matters. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Obedience is only in what is right.” Narrated by al-Bukhārī (7257) and Muslim (1840). He also established an exception concerning “clear disbelief for which you have proof from Allah.” Narrated by al-Bukhārī (7056) and Muslim (1709).

Thus, injustice must be opposed according to knowledge, ability, and lawful means, while considering likely benefits and harms and avoiding greater evil. Preventing greater harm does not justify oppression or extinguish the rights of those wronged. Equally, the duty to oppose injustice does not make every proposed means of removing it permissible. And Allah knows best.)
Enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is a communal obligation. If some people fulfill it, the obligation falls from the rest. If everyone abandons it, then everyone capable of carrying it out without a valid excuse bears sin.
It becomes an individual obligation upon the one who is able to remove the wrongdoing, such as someone who sees his wife, children, or servant committing a wrong.
Wrongdoing should be condemned in matters upon which the scholars have reached consensus.
As for matters genuinely disputed among the scholars, they are not condemned in the same manner, because according to one position every qualified mujtahid is correct, and this is the view preferred by many verifying scholars. According to the other position, only one view is correct, but the mistaken party is not necessarily identifiable to us, and he is not sinful for his qualified error.
Scholars and ordinary Muslims alike may participate in matters whose rulings are clear and apparent, such as commanding prayer and fasting and forbidding fornication, drinking alcohol, assault, insults, and similar matters.
If, however, the matter concerns subtle details of actions and speech or issues requiring juristic interpretation, ordinary people have no role in that; rather, it belongs to the scholars alone.
The one who enjoins right and forbids wrong has no right to investigate, search, spy, or enter people’s homes merely on the basis of suspicion.
An exception is when a trustworthy person informs him of an imminent grave wrong, such as a man isolating another person in order to kill him, being alone with a woman in order to commit fornication with her, or selling intoxicants and hashish. In such a case, investigation and intervention may be permitted in order to prevent an irreversible harm.
The Prophet’s ﷺ words:
“If he cannot, then with his heart”
mean that he should reject the wrongdoing inwardly and not approve of it.
This does not physically remove or change the wrongdoing, but it is what lies within his ability.
This hadith also indicates, according to the strongest view among the scholars, that if a person fears for himself being killed, beaten, or driven away, the obligation of physically changing the wrongdoing falls from him.
The author states that correction of wrongdoing should be carried out privately.
Sulaymān al-Khawwāṣ said:
“Whoever admonishes his brother privately, between himself and him, has sincerely advised him. Whoever admonishes him publicly before the people has only exposed and disgraced him.”
Narrated by Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Amr bi-al-Maʿrūf wa-al-Nahy ʿan al-Munkar (58).
